citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $\nu>0$, $1/2<\alpha\le3/4$, and nonnegative $\eta\in C^\infty([0,\infty))$ supported in $[0,1/16)$ and equal to $1$ on $[0,1/32]$. Define $w_0(y)=\eta(y)y^{-1/2}(\log(1/y))^{-\alpha}$ for $0<y<1/16$, and $w_0(y)=0$ for $y\ge1/16$. Put
$$G_t(s)=(4\pi\nu t)^{-1/2}e^{-s^2/(4\nu t)},$$
$$w(t,y)=\int_0^\infty[G_t(y-z)-G_t(y+z)]w_0(z)\,dz.$$
Then $w_0\in L^1\cap L^2(0,\infty)$, $w\ge0$, $w(t,0)=0$, $w_t=\nu w_{yy}$, and $w$ is smooth for positive time, including at $y=0$. Moreover
$$\sup_{t>0}\|w(t)\|_j\le\|w_0\|_j\quad(j=1,2),\qquad w(t)\to w_0\text{ in }L^2\text{ as }t\downarrow0,$$
$$\int_0^T\|w_y(t)\|_2^2\,dt\le(2\nu)^{-1}\|w_0\|_2^2,\qquad \int_0^T\|w(t)\|_4^4\,dt<\infty.$$
Write $M(t)=\int_0^\infty w(t,y)\,dy$, $M_0=\int_0^\infty w_0$, $m(t)=M(t)-M_0$, and $h(t,y)=-\int_y^\infty w(t,z)\,dz$. Then $h_y=w$, $h_t=\nu h_{yy}$, $h(t,0)=-M(t)$, and $m(0)=0$. For some $t_*>0$ and $c,C>0$, writing $L(t)=\log(1/t)$,
$$c t^{-3/4}L(t)^{-\alpha}\le -m'(t)\le C t^{-3/4}L(t)^{-\alpha},\qquad |m(t)|\le C t^{1/4}L(t)^{-\alpha}\quad(0<t<t_*).$$
Consequently $m'\in L^1(0,T)\setminus L^{4/3}(0,T)$ and
$$\int_0^T\bigl(|m'(t)|t^{1/4}+|m(t)|t^{-3/4}\bigr)^2\,dt<\infty$$
for every finite $T>0$. On each bounded $y$ interval, $h(t,\cdot)\to h_0(\cdot)=-\int_{\cdot}^\infty w_0$ uniformly as $t\downarrow0$. On each closed interval separated from $\operatorname{supp}w_0$, all spatial derivatives of $w$ are bounded for small positive time by $C_Nt^{-N}e^{-c/t}$, with constants allowed to depend on the derivative.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D=(0,1)^2$, $b\in C^\infty(\overline D)$ vanish on $\partial D$, and choose $\rho\in C^\infty([0,\infty))$ equal to $1$ on $[0,1/3]$ and $0$ on $[1,\infty)$. Set $d_1=x$, $d_2=1-x$, $d_3=y$, $d_4=1-y$, and
$$R_\ell(x,y)=1-\prod_{i=1}^4(1-\rho(d_i/\ell)),\qquad 0<\ell<1/16.$$
This function is $1$ near the boundary and supported in strips of total area at most $4\ell$. There is $C$, independent of $\ell$, such that
$$\|\nabla(bR_\ell)\|_\infty\le C,\qquad \|D^k(bR_\ell)\|_2\le C\ell^{3/2-k}\quad(k=1,2,3).$$
For $\ell(t)=\sqrt t$, $0<t<T<1/256$,
$$\|\partial_t\nabla(bR_{\sqrt t})\|_2\le Ct^{-1}t^{1/4}.$$
If $m\in C^1((0,T))$, $\operatorname{rot}\psi=(\psi_y,-\psi_x)$, and $r=-m\operatorname{rot}(bR_{\sqrt t})$, then
$$\|r\|_\infty\le C|m|,\quad \|r\|_2\le C|m|t^{1/4},\quad \|\nabla r\|_2\le C|m|t^{-1/4},$$
$$\|r_t\|_2+\|\Delta r\|_2\le C(|m'|t^{1/4}+|m|t^{-3/4}).$$
Moreover $bR_\ell=0$ and $\partial_n(bR_\ell)=\partial_n b$ on each side. Thus if a smooth stream $\Psi$ has zero boundary value and $\partial_n\Psi=m\partial_n b$, then $\Psi-mbR_\ell$ has both zero value and zero normal derivative there, and its rotation has zero velocity trace. On any fixed $J\Subset(0,1)$ and sufficiently small $t$, the additional estimate $\|\partial_xr\|_{L^\infty(J\times(0,1))}\le C_J|m|$ holds.

Assume Countable Choice as inherited from [[def-na-evolutionary-incompressible-ns-weak-solution]]. Let $D$, $V$, $Q$, $V_\sigma$, $H_\sigma$, $a_\nu$, and $c$ be as in [[def-na-evolutionary-incompressible-ns-weak-solution]]; the Stokes velocity and pressure spaces are $V=H^1_0(D)^d$ and $Q=L^2_0(D)$ as specified in [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]]. For $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2(D)^d)$ and $u_0\in H_\sigma$, a **solenoidal energy weak velocity** is a velocity $u\in L^\infty(0,T;H_\sigma)\cap L^2(0,T;V_\sigma)$ that is weakly continuous into $H_\sigma$, satisfies $\operatorname{div}u=0$ almost everywhere, and obeys the scalar-test weak equation
$$-\int_0^T(u(t),v)_{L^2}\eta'(t)\,dt+\int_0^T\big(a_\nu(u(t),v)+c(u(t);u(t),v)\big)\eta(t)\,dt=\int_0^T(f(t),v)_{L^2}\eta(t)\,dt+(u_0,v)_{L^2}\eta(0)$$
for every fixed $v\in V_\sigma$ and $\eta\in C^1([0,T])$ vanishing near $T$. It also satisfies, for almost every $t\in(0,T)$,
$$\frac12\|u(t)\|_{L^2}^2+\nu\int_0^t\|\nabla u(s)\|_{L^2}^2\,ds\le\frac12\|u_0\|_{L^2}^2+\int_0^t(f(s),u(s))_{L^2}\,ds.$$
This solenoidal definition does not itself assert a pressure exists in $L^{4/3}(0,T;L^2_0(D))$; that is a separate regularity conclusion.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz open set, where Lipschitz means that $\partial D$ has a finite rigidly moved graph-chart atlas. Here $H^1_0(D)$ is the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(D)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). Since $D$ has finite measure, Holder makes every $L^2$ class integrable, so the zero-mean condition is well-defined ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]). Define
$$V:=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q:=L^2_0(D):=\{q\in L^2(D;\mathbb R):\int_Dq=0\}.$$
Equip $V$ with $\|v\|_V:=\|
abla v\|_{L^2(D)}$ and $Q$ with $\|q\|_Q:=\|q\|_{L^2(D)}$. The local Poincare inequality [[lem-na-homogeneous-dirichlet-poincare]] makes the first a norm equivalent to the usual $H^1$ norm. For $v\in V$, define $\varepsilon(v):=(
abla v+
abla v^T)/2$ and $b(v,q):=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v$. For viscosity $
u>0$, set $a_
u(u,v):=2
u\int_D\varepsilon(u):\varepsilon(v)$, where $X:Y=\sum_{i,j}X_{ij}Y_{ij}$. The continuous domain class is all bounded connected Lipschitz $D$; the exact mini-element mesh class is the narrower polygonal/polyhedral conforming affine simplicial class.

Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded connected Lipschitz domain with $d\in\{2,3\}$, and let $V=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ as in [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]]. For $a,b,c\in V$, define the real **skew convective form**
$$c(a;b,c):= rac12\int_D ig((a\cdot
abla)b\cdot c-(a\cdot
abla)c\cdot b ig)\,dx.$$
The middle and last slots are displayed separately to emphasize $c(a;b,c)=-c(a;c,b)$. In particular $c(a;b,b)=0$. The integrals are well-defined on $V$ by [[lem-na-evolutionary-skew-convective-form-bound]]. If additionally $\operatorname{div}a=0$, then $c(a;b,c)=\int_D(a\cdot
abla)b\cdot c$.
Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open. If $v\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, then $\operatorname{div}v\in L^2(D)$ and $\int_D\operatorname{div}v=0$.

Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and Lipschitz, with $d\in\{2,3\}$. Under Countable Choice there is a bounded linear map $B_D:L^2_0(D)\to H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ such that
$$\operatorname{div}B_Dq=q,\qquad \|\nabla B_Dq\|_2\le C_{\rm div}(D)\|q\|_2.$$
For a chosen finite cover and tree decomposition from [[lem-na-lipschitz-domain-finite-star-shaped-cover]] and [[lem-na-finite-cover-zero-mean-data-decomposition]], one valid bound is $C_{\rm div}(D)=\sum_i C_{U_i}D_i$; it is finite and independent of any finite-element mesh.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d\in\{2,3\}$, be nonempty, bounded, connected, Lipschitz and polyhedral, and let $0<T<\infty$. Let $\{\mathcal T_j\}$ be matching shape-regular affine simplicial meshes with $h_j\to0$, and let the time partitions of $[0,T]$ have maximum step tending to zero, with no relation required between the two limits. Let $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2(D)^d)$ and $u_0\in H_\sigma$. On each mesh take $u_j^0=P_{Z_j}u_0$, the $L^2$-orthogonal projection onto the weak MINI kernel, and choose any backward Euler MINI solution from [[thm-na-mini-be-step-existence-energy]]. Then a subsequence of piecewise-constant velocities converges strongly in $L^2(0,T;L^2(D)^d)$ and weakly in $L^2(0,T;H^1_0(D)^d)$ to a velocity $u$ satisfying the solenoidal weak momentum equation, initial trace and energy inequality in [[def-na-solenoidal-energy-weak-ns-velocity]]. This theorem supplies the velocity limit and its energy inequality. It does not assert the pressure regularity and pressure-bearing formulation required by the PE06 plan; the remaining pressure obligation is explicitly escalated on the A page.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^2$ be bounded, connected and Lipschitz, $T>0$, $\nu>0$, $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2(D)^2)$ and $u_0\in H_\sigma$. There is at most one solenoidal energy weak velocity in the sense of [[def-na-solenoidal-energy-weak-ns-velocity]] for these data. Every such velocity belongs to $L^4(0,T;L^4(D)^2)\cap C([0,T];H_\sigma)$ and has its actual restricted derivative in $L^2(0,T;V_\sigma^*)$. The continuity is strong, its initial value is $u_0$, and its solenoidal evolution equation satisfies the Hilbert-triple energy chain rule. No full nonsolenoidal $V^*$ derivative or regular instantaneous pressure is asserted.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

derivations.claim: The choices in **Given** exist by [F8]: take a bump centered at $1/2$ with inner radius $1/24$ and outer radius $1/12$ for $a$, giving a nonzero function compactly supported in $(1/3,2/3)$. Restrict zero-centered bumps to the positive halfline with radii $(1/32,1/16)$ for $\eta$, $(1/8,1/4)$ for $\kappa$ and $\chi$, and $(1/3,1)$ for $\rho$. They have every stated support, plateau and sign property. Put $a_n=2\int_0^1a(x)\sin(n\pi x)\,dx$ and define $$\theta(x,y)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_n\sin(n\pi x)\frac{\sinh(n\pi(1-y))}{\sinh(n\pi)},\qquad \widetilde\phi(x,y)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_n\cos(n\pi x)\frac{\cosh(n\pi(1-y))}{\sinh(n\pi)}.$$ Repeated integration by parts makes $|a_n|\le C_Nn^{-N}$ for every $N$, since $a$ vanishes near the endpoints. The hyperbolic factors and their derivatives of order $k$ are bounded by $C_kn^k$ uniformly on $[0,1]$. Thus every differentiated series converges absolutely uniformly, and both functions are smooth on the closed square and harmonic. The sine series equals $a$ at $y=0$: indeed the odd, $2$-periodic smooth extension of $a$ has its Fourier series equal to itself. To verify this last assertion directly, its rapid coefficients define a uniformly convergent Fourier series with the same coefficients; their difference has all Fourier coefficients zero. Convolution with the Fejer kernels, which are nonnegative unit-mass kernels concentrating at zero by their formula $N^{-1}|\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}e^{ij\pi x}|^2$, converges uniformly to a continuous periodic function by uniform continuity; it vanishes for a function whose coefficients all vanish. Hence the difference is zero. The other boundary values of $\theta$ are zero. Direct differentiation gives $\widetilde\phi_x=\theta_y$ and $\widetilde\phi_y=-\theta_x$. Let $\phi=\widetilde\phi-\int_D\widetilde\phi$, so $\phi\in Q$, $\nabla\phi=\operatorname{rot}\theta$, and $\|\phi\|_2>0$ because $a\ne0$ makes $\theta$ nonconstant.

Define $b=\theta-a\chi$. This is smooth and zero on all four sides. Its normal derivative equals $\partial_n\theta$ everywhere on the boundary: at the bottom $\chi'=0$, at the top $\chi=\chi'=0$, and near the vertical sides $a=a'=0$. Take the function $R(t)=R_{\sqrt t}$ from [F2] and choose $T$ small enough for that construction, with $\sqrt T<1/16$. Set $$\psi_m=a(x)[\kappa(y)h(t,y)+M_0\chi(y)],\qquad \psi=\psi_m+m(t)\theta-m(t)bR(t),$$ $$u=\operatorname{rot}\psi,\qquad p=-m'(t)\phi,\qquad r=-m(t)\operatorname{rot}(bR(t)).$$ All these fields are smooth for $t>0$. On the bottom $\psi_m=-am$, $\theta=a$, and $b=0$; on the other sides $\psi_m=\theta=b=0$. Thus $\psi=0$ on the boundary. The normal derivative of $\psi_m$ is zero on every side: on the bottom it is, up to its sign, $a w(t,0)=0$, and on all other sides the fixed cutoffs or $a,a'$ vanish. Hence $\partial_n(\psi_m+m\theta)=m\partial_n b$, and [F2] makes $\partial_n\psi=0$. Thus $u(t)\in V_\sigma$ exactly, with no-slip on every edge including compatible corner values.

Write $L(t)=\log(1/t)$. By [F1] and [F2], $$\|r\|_\infty\le C|m|,\quad \|r\|_2\le C|m|t^{1/4},\quad \|\nabla r\|_2\le C|m|t^{-1/4},$$ $$\|r_t\|_2+\|\Delta r\|_2\le C(|m'|t^{1/4}+|m|t^{-3/4})\le Ct^{-1/2}L(t)^{-\alpha}.$$ The last function is square integrable near zero because $2\alpha>1$. In particular $r\in L^\infty_tL^2_x\cap L^2_tH^1_x$ and $r(t)\to0$ strongly in $L^2$. The main stream rotation has a uniform $L^2$ bound from bounded $h$ and bounded $\|w\|_2$. Its gradient uses only bounded $h$, $w$ with fixed coefficients and $w_y$ with fixed coefficients, so the heat energy bound makes it $L^2_{t,x}$. The smooth field $m\operatorname{rot}\theta$ has the same required bounds. We obtain $$u\in L^\infty(0,T;L^2(D)^2)\cap L^2(0,T;V_\sigma).$$

The outer harmonic field cancels the entire rough gradient: $(\partial_t-
u\Delta)(m\operatorname{rot}	heta)+
abla p=m'
abla\phi-m'
abla\phi=0$. The main stream has the explicit residual $$(\partial_t-
u\Delta)\psi_m=-
u[a''\kappa h+2a\kappa'w+a\kappa''h]-
u M_0[a''\chi+a\chi''].$$ Its rotation contains only fixed coefficients times $h,w$, except for terms with $\kappa'w_y$. The latter are supported in $y\ge1/8$, a fixed positive distance from $\operatorname{supp}w_0\subset[0,1/16]$, and are square integrable by the off-support Gaussian bound in [F1]. All other terms are uniformly $L^2$ bounded. Together with step 3.1 this proves $$F_L=(\partial_t-
u\Delta)u+
abla p\in L^2(0,T;L^2(D)^2).$$

Let $h_0(y)=-\int_y^\infty w_0(z)\,dz$, $\psi_0=a[\kappa h_0+M_0\chi]$, and $u_0=\operatorname{rot}\psi_0$. Strong $L^2$ convergence of $w$, uniform convergence of $h$ on $[0,1]$, $m(t)\to0$ and step 3.1 give $u(t)\to u_0$ strongly in $L^2$. The stream $\psi_0$ is $H^1$, supported away from the other three sides, and vanishes on the bottom because $h_0(0)=-M_0$. Here is a direct approximation proving $\psi_0\in H^1_0$, without relying on an unstated trace theorem. Near the bottom it equals $a(x)\int_0^yw_0(z)\,dz$. If a cutoff removes $0<y<\varepsilon$, the derivative-of-cutoff error is bounded in squared $L^2$ by $$C\varepsilon^{-2}\int_0^{2\varepsilon}\left|\int_0^yw_0(z)\,dz\right|^2dy\le C\int_0^{2\varepsilon}|w_0(z)|^2\,dz\longrightarrow0.$$ The inequality follows from $|\int_0^y w_0|^2\le y\int_0^y|w_0|^2$ and integrating $y\le2\varepsilon$. The other errors tend to zero by absolute continuity of the integrals of $|\psi_0|^2+|\nabla\psi_0|^2$. The cut-off streams are smooth and compactly supported inside $D$, since $w_0$ is smooth away from zero. Their rotations belong to $V_\sigma$ and converge to $u_0$ in $L^2$, proving $u_0\in H_\sigma$ by its actual closure definition.

The normal component $u_2$ is uniformly bounded in space and time: $-\partial_x\psi_m$ uses only bounded $h$ and fixed functions, the harmonic term has bounded amplitude $m$, and $r$ is uniformly bounded. Thus $u_2\partial_yu\in L^2_{t,x}$ by step 3.1. The only unbounded part of $u_1$ is $a\kappa w$. Choose $J\Subset(0,1)$ containing $\operatorname{supp}a$ and decrease $T$ so the last estimate in [F2] applies there. On $J	imes(0,1)$, $\partial_xr$ is uniformly bounded; the main and harmonic terms satisfy $|\partial_xu|\le C(1+|w|)$, so $|u_1\partial_xu|\le C(1+|w|^2)$. This belongs to $L^2_{t,x}$ by $w\in L^4_{t,y}$. Outside $J$, the coefficient $a$ vanishes and $u_1$ is bounded, so $u_1\partial_xu\in L^2_{t,x}$ there by the energy-gradient bound. Hence $N(u)=(u\cdot
abla)u\in L^2_{t,x}$. Define $f=F_L+N(u)$. It belongs to $L^2_tL^2_x$, and the pointwise positive-time equation is $u_t-
u\Delta u+N(u)+
abla p=f$.

On $[\varepsilon,T]$, integrate the smooth equation from step 5.1 against $u$. The convection and pressure integrals vanish by divergence and no slip. Thus $$\tfrac12\|u(t)\|_2^2+\nu\int_\varepsilon^t\|\nabla u\|_2^2=\tfrac12\|u(\varepsilon)\|_2^2+\int_\varepsilon^t(f,u).$$ Let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$: strong initial convergence handles the endpoint and the energy and force bounds handle both integrals. This gives energy equality with initial value $u_0$. Similarly integrate the positive-time equation against a fixed solenoidal $V$ test and a smooth scalar time test, integrate by parts in time, and send $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The pressure term vanishes; all remaining integrals converge by the established bounds. The resulting identity is precisely the solenoidal weak equation with initial value $u_0$. Positive-time smoothness and strong initial convergence give the required weak continuity on $[0,T]$. Thus $u$ is a solenoidal energy weak velocity of [F3].

The pressure has zero spatial mean and is in $L^1_tQ$, since $m'\in L^1$ and $\phi\in Q$. It defines a time-distribution pressure for the full momentum equation: test the pointwise equation on compact positive-time intervals; its time-distribution identity on $(0,T)$ follows directly. Also $\|p(t)\|_2=|m'(t)|\|\phi\|_2$, so [F1] and $\|\phi\|_2>0$ imply $p\notin L^{4/3}_tQ$. If a second mean-zero $Q$-valued pressure distribution $q$ represented this same velocity and force, subtract their momentum equations. For each scalar time test $\zeta$, the $Q$ element $\langle q-p,\zeta\rangle$ has zero divergence pairing with every $V$ test. Pair with the bounded divergence right inverse of that very element, using [F4], to show its squared norm is zero. Thus $q=p$ as $Q$-valued distributions. In particular, if $q\in L^{4/3}_tQ$, both are $L^1_tQ$ functions and equality of their distributions gives equality almost everywhere (test against a countable dense set in $Q$ and scalar tests), contradicting the nonintegrability just proved. Consequently this velocity does not meet the regular-pressure definition named in the Counterexample.

By [[lem-na-two-dimensional-solenoidal-energy-velocity-uniqueness]], the constructed solenoidal energy velocity is the unique one for these two-dimensional square data. Every actual MINI subsequential limit supplied by [F5] is a solenoidal energy weak velocity with these same data, hence equals $u$. Steps 1.1–5.1 give all concrete properties and show that no mean-zero endpoint-integrable pressure exists for that limit. This refutes the universal regular-pressure assertion.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. For every $t>0$: (i) $\Gamma(\cdot,t)>0$
and $\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x,t)\,dx=1$; (ii) parabolic scaling:
$\Gamma(\lambda x,\lambda^2t)=\lambda^{-n}\Gamma(x,t)$ for every $\lambda>0$ and
$x\in\mathbb R^n$; (iii) $\Gamma$ is $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$ and solves the heat equation there,
$\partial_t\Gamma(x,t)=\Delta_x\Gamma(x,t)$; (iv) for every multi-index $\alpha$
there is $C_{n,\alpha}<\infty$ with
$|D^\alpha_x\Gamma(x,t)|\le C_{n,\alpha}t^{-(|\alpha|+n)/2}e^{-|x|^2/(8t)}$ for
all $x\in\mathbb R^n$, $t>0$; in particular $\|\Gamma(\cdot,t)\|_1=1$ and
$(\Gamma(\cdot,t))_{t>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity on $\mathbb R^n$.

Assume Countable Choice. For $n\ge1$, the kernels $\Gamma_t$ are positive with
unit mass and $\|\Gamma_t\|_1=1$. For every $\delta>0$,
$\int_{|x|>\delta}\Gamma(x,t)\,dx\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$. Thus they form an
$L^1$ approximate identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $1 \le p,q,r \le \infty$ satisfy

$$ \frac1r = \frac1p + \frac1q - 1. $$

If $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $g \in L^q(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then the
convolution $f*g$ is defined almost everywhere and satisfies

$$ \|f*g\|_r \le \|f\|_p\|g\|_q. $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

derivations.claim: The square of $w_0$ near zero is $y^{-1}(\log(1/y))^{-2\alpha}$, integrable because $2\alpha>1$; its first power is also integrable. For $y,z>0$, $G_t(y-z)\ge G_t(y+z)$, proving positivity. Its integral in either positive variable is at most $1$. Thus the positive kernel is an $L^1$ contraction; Jensen's inequality in its subprobability measure, followed by integration in $y$, proves the $L^2$ contraction. Equivalently the latter follows by Young applied to the odd extension $\widetilde w_0$ on the line, whose heat evolution remains odd; restricting the equal two halfline norms gives the same bound. The Gaussian derivative bounds justify differentiating the convolution for every $t>0$, and give $w_t=\nu w_{yy}$ and the zero boundary value. Approximate-identity convergence applied to $\widetilde w_0$ gives strong $L^2$ initial convergence.

Fix a smooth $\beta:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]$ equal to $0$ on $[0,1]$ and $1$ on $[2,\infty)$. The explicit $w_{0,j}(y)=\beta(jy)w_0(y)$ are smooth and compactly supported away from zero and converge to $w_0$ in $L^2$ by dominated convergence. Evolve their odd extensions. Integration by parts on the line, with Gaussian tails, gives $\|w(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_0^t\|w_y\|_2^2=\|w_0\|_2^2$ for each approximant. Applying this identity to differences makes the evolutions Cauchy in $L^\infty_tL^2_y$ and their derivatives Cauchy in $L^2_{t,y}$. Their limit is the kernel evolution by its contraction, and its weak derivative is the derivative limit by integration against compactly supported tests. This gives the stated energy inequality. For a smooth halfline function vanishing at zero and decaying at infinity, the fundamental theorem gives $\|w\|_\infty^2\le2\|w\|_2\|w_y\|_2$, hence $\|w\|_4^4\le2\|w\|_2^3\|w_y\|_2$. Time integration, the energy bound and Holder prove the $L^4$ assertion; approximation passes the inequality to this $w$.

Integrating the Gaussian kernel first in $y$ gives $M(t)=\int_0^\infty\operatorname{erf}(z/(2\sqrt{
u t}))w_0(z)\,dz$, where $\operatorname{erf}(r)=2\pi^{-1/2}\int_0^r e^{-s^2}\,ds$. Dominated convergence gives $M(t)	o M_0$, and differentiation for positive time gives $$m'(t)=- rac{t^{-3/2}}{2\sqrt{\pi
u}}\int_0^\infty z e^{-z^2/(4
u t)}w_0(z)\,dz.$$ After $z=\sqrt t\,r$, the prefactor is $t^{-3/4}$. The integral on $1\le r\le2$ is bounded below by $cL(t)^{-\alpha}$ for small $t$. For $r\le t^{-1/4}$, $\log(1/(\sqrt t r))\ge L(t)/4$, so the integral is bounded above by $CL(t)^{-\alpha}\int_0^\infty r^{1/2}e^{-r^2/(4
u)}\,dr$. For $r>t^{-1/4}$ the Gaussian tail is exponentially small; on the support of $\eta(\sqrt t r)$ the logarithmic factor is uniformly bounded above, which gives the same upper bound. This proves both derivative bounds. Integrating the upper bound from zero gives $|m(t)|\le Ct^{1/4}L(t)^{-\alpha}$.

The upper derivative bound is integrable. The lower bound gives $\int_0^{t_*}|m'|^{4/3}\ge c\int_0^{t_*}t^{-1}L(t)^{-4\alpha/3}\,dt=\infty$, since $4\alpha/3\le1$. In contrast the squared critical-corrector expression is at most $Ct^{-1}L(t)^{-2\alpha}$, which is integrable since $2\alpha>1$. Away from time zero every quantity is smooth, proving all stated time-integral conclusions.

Differentiating the tail integral gives $h_y=w$ and $h_t=\nu w_y=\nu h_{yy}$; the boundary term at infinity vanishes by Gaussian decay. Also $h(t,y)=\int_0^yw(t,z)\,dz-M(t)$. Thus on $[0,B]$ its difference from $h_0$ is at most $\sqrt B\|w(t)-w_0\|_2+|M(t)-M_0|$, which tends to zero. Finally a positive separation between $y$ and $\operatorname{supp}w_0$ puts every differentiated Gaussian convolution under the bound $C_Nt^{-N}e^{-c/t}\|w_0\|_1$. These arguments prove the remaining assertions.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a bounded connected Lipschitz polygonal/polyhedral domain with a conforming shape-regular simplicial mesh, $d=2$ or $3$, mesh size $h=\max_Kh_K$. For each interior mesh vertex $z$, choose any incident facet $F_z$; for each boundary vertex choose an incident boundary facet. Let $\psi_{z,F_z}\in P_1(F_z)$ be the unique dual affine function satisfying $\int_{F_z}\psi_{z,F_z}\varphi_y=\delta_{zy}$ for the facet's P1 nodal basis. Define
$$I_hv=\sum_z\left(\int_{F_z}\psi_{z,F_z}\operatorname{tr}v\right)\varphi_z.$$
This is a linear face-average interpolant $H^1(D)\to S_h$, where $S_h$ is the continuous piecewise P1 space. It maps $H^1_0(D)$ into $S_h\cap H^1_0(D)$, is uniformly $H^1$-seminorm stable, and for each element patch $\omega_K$ has
$$\|v-I_hv\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}.$$
If $v\in H^2(D)$, then $\|\nabla(v-I_hv)\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. Constants depend only on dimension, the fixed domain, and the mesh shape-regularity bound. No point evaluation is used.

On the mini-element spaces of [[def-na-mini-element-p1-bubble-p1-spaces]], there is a Fortin operator $\Pi_h:V\to V_h$ preserving $b(v,q_h)$ for every $q_h\in Q_h$, with $\|\Pi_hv\|_V\le C_F\|v\|_V$. The constant depends only on $d$ and the mesh shape-regularity bound, not on $h$. Consequently
$$\beta_h\ge (C_FC_{\rm div}(D))^{-1}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a bounded connected Lipschitz polygonal/polyhedral domain with a conforming shape-regular simplicial mesh, $d=2$ or $3$, mesh size $h=\max_Kh_K$. For each interior mesh vertex $z$, choose any incident facet $F_z$; for each boundary vertex choose an incident boundary facet. Let $\psi_{z,F_z}\in P_1(F_z)$ be the unique dual affine function satisfying $\int_{F_z}\psi_{z,F_z}\varphi_y=\delta_{zy}$ for the facet's P1 nodal basis. Define
$$I_hv=\sum_z\left(\int_{F_z}\psi_{z,F_z}\operatorname{tr}v\right)\varphi_z.$$
This is a linear face-average interpolant $H^1(D)\to S_h$, where $S_h$ is the continuous piecewise P1 space. It maps $H^1_0(D)$ into $S_h\cap H^1_0(D)$, is uniformly $H^1$-seminorm stable, and for each element patch $\omega_K$ has
$$\|v-I_hv\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}.$$
If $v\in H^2(D)$, then $\|\nabla(v-I_hv)\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. Constants depend only on dimension, the fixed domain, and the mesh shape-regularity bound. No point evaluation is used.

On the mini-element spaces of [[def-na-mini-element-p1-bubble-p1-spaces]], there is a Fortin operator $\Pi_h:V\to V_h$ preserving $b(v,q_h)$ for every $q_h\in Q_h$, with $\|\Pi_hv\|_V\le C_F\|v\|_V$. The constant depends only on $d$ and the mesh shape-regularity bound, not on $h$. Consequently
$$\beta_h\ge (C_FC_{\rm div}(D))^{-1}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d=2$ or $3$, be a bounded connected Lipschitz polygonal/polyhedral domain with a conforming shape-regular affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$. On a simplex $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_d$, define the scalar interior bubble $b_K=(d+1)^{d+1}\prod_{i=0}^d\lambda_i$. Let
$$S^1_h=\{w\in C^0(\overline D):w|_K\in P_1(K)\},\quad S^1_{h,0}=S^1_h\cap H^1_0(D).$$
The **mini-element spaces** are
$$V_h=[S^1_{h,0}]^d\oplus\bigoplus_{K\in\mathcal T_h}b_K\mathbb R^d\subset H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q_h=S^1_h\cap L^2_0(D).$$
Each bubble is extended by zero off its cell. The zero-boundary conformity of the piecewise affine part is supplied by [[thm-zero-boundary-piecewise-polynomials-in-w10p]]. The local/global dimensions are proved in the next dimension lemma.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz open set, where Lipschitz means that $\partial D$ has a finite rigidly moved graph-chart atlas. Here $H^1_0(D)$ is the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(D)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). Since $D$ has finite measure, Holder makes every $L^2$ class integrable, so the zero-mean condition is well-defined ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]). Define
$$V:=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q:=L^2_0(D):=\{q\in L^2(D;\mathbb R):\int_Dq=0\}.$$
Equip $V$ with $\|v\|_V:=\|
abla v\|_{L^2(D)}$ and $Q$ with $\|q\|_Q:=\|q\|_{L^2(D)}$. The local Poincare inequality [[lem-na-homogeneous-dirichlet-poincare]] makes the first a norm equivalent to the usual $H^1$ norm. For $v\in V$, define $\varepsilon(v):=(
abla v+
abla v^T)/2$ and $b(v,q):=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v$. For viscosity $
u>0$, set $a_
u(u,v):=2
u\int_D\varepsilon(u):\varepsilon(v)$, where $X:Y=\sum_{i,j}X_{ij}Y_{ij}$. The continuous domain class is all bounded connected Lipschitz $D$; the exact mini-element mesh class is the narrower polygonal/polyhedral conforming affine simplicial class.

For the conforming mini-element spaces $V_h,Q_h$, define the **weak discrete divergence kernel** by
$$Z_h:=\{v_h\in V_h:b(v_h,q_h)=0\text{ for every }q_h\in Q_h\},$$
and the **exact discrete divergence kernel** by
$$Z_h^0:=\{v_h\in V_h:\operatorname{div}v_h=0\text{ almost everywhere on }D\}.$$
Since $b(v_h,q_h)=-\int_Dq_h\operatorname{div}v_h$, one has $Z_h^0\subseteq Z_h$. Equality is not part of either definition; the companion example proves strictness for a concrete mesh.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero

Apply this componentwise and sum squares for vector $v$. The local gradient bound $\|\nabla(v-I_hv)\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$ is also [F1]. All these estimates use facet averages and require no representative with point values.

Write $e_K=v-I_hv$ on $K$. The actual numerator of the Fortin coefficient is the unweighted integral of $e_K$, so [F3] and [F5] give $|c_K|\le |K|^{1/2}(\int_Kb_K)^{-1}\|e_K\|_{L^2(K)}\le C|K|^{-1/2}\|e_K\|_{L^2(K)}$. Hence $\|b_Kc_K\|_{L^2(K)}\le C\|e_K\|_{L^2(K)}$ and $\|\nabla(b_Kc_K)\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K^{-1}\|e_K\|_{L^2(K)}$. No bound involving a global inverse mesh scale is used.

Bubble interiors are disjoint, so on $K$ the existing map satisfies $v-\Pi_hv=e_K-b_Kc_K$. Square and sum the two estimates in step 2.1. Since $h_K\le h$ and the patch overlap is uniformly bounded by [F1], $\sum_Kh_K^4\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}^2\le Ch^4\|D^2v\|_2^2$ and $\sum_Kh_K^2\|D^2v\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}^2\le Ch^2\|D^2v\|_2^2$. Suppose $v\in H^2(D)^d\cap V_\sigma$. Because $Q_h\subset L^2_0(D)$, [F4] gives $b(v,q_h)=0$ for every $q_h\in Q_h$. Fortin preservation [F2] therefore puts $\Pi_hv\in Z_h$. Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

derivations.claim: The product formula shows that $R_\ell=1$ whenever some $d_i<\ell/3$, and $R_\ell=0$ whenever every $d_i\ge\ell$. The supporting union has area at most $4\ell$. Smoothness follows from the finite product. Because $b=0$ on each side, the fundamental theorem in its normal coordinate gives $|b(x,y)|\le C d_i(x,y)$ for every side $i$, and $\nabla b$ and all fixed higher derivatives are bounded on the closed square.

Expand $D^k(bR_\ell)$ by the product rule. Every spatial derivative on a cutoff costs at most $C\ell^{-1}$. If at least one cutoff is differentiated, choose that side $i$; on that term's support $d_i\le\ell$, so an undifferentiated $b$ supplies a factor $C\ell$. Thus the terms with no derivative on $b$ have magnitude at most $C\ell^{1-k}$. If $j\ge1$ derivatives hit $b$, the other factors cost at most $C\ell^{-(k-j)}\le C\ell^{1-k}$. Terms with no differentiated cutoff have the same bound for $k\ge1$. All terms are supported in the union from step 1.1. Therefore $\|D^k(bR_\ell)\|_2\le C\ell^{3/2-k}$ for $k=1,2,3$; for $k=1$ the pointwise bound also gives $\|\nabla(bR_\ell)\|_\infty\le C$. Intersections of strips require no disjointness: the bound uses any differentiated side and the total union area.

With $\ell=\sqrt t$, a time derivative of $\rho(d_i/\ell)$ is bounded by $Ct^{-1}$ and is supported where $d_i\le\ell$. One extra spatial derivative costs at most $C\ell^{-1}$, offset by $b=O(\ell)$ if it does not hit $b$. If it hits $b$, its derivative is bounded. Hence $|\partial_t\nabla(bR_{\sqrt t})|\le Ct^{-1}$ on the same union of strips, and its $L^2$ norm is at most $Ct^{-1}\ell^{1/2}$. Differentiating $r$ and applying step 2.1 with $k=1,2,3$ gives every asserted bound for $r$, $r_t$ and $\Delta r$.

Near each boundary point $R_\ell=1$, so the boundary value of $bR_\ell$ is zero and its normal derivative equals that of $b$. Subtraction therefore cancels the stated stream trace and normal derivative. The tangential derivative of a zero boundary stream is zero, so its rotation has both zero normal and zero tangential velocity on each side. For $x\in J$ and sufficiently small $t$, the cutoffs of the vertical sides vanish identically and $R$ depends only on $y$. Since $b(x,0)=b(x,1)=0$, also $b_x,b_{xx}$ vanish on those edges and satisfy $|b_x|+|b_{xx}|\le C\min(y,1-y)$. Consequently $\partial_xr=-m\operatorname{rot}(b_xR)$ is bounded by $C_J|m|$: the only factor $R_y=O(\ell^{-1})$ is multiplied by $b_x=O(\ell)$ in its supporting strip. This proves the last estimate and completes the proof.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: For scalar $z\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ the coordinate fundamental theorem gives $|z(x,y)|^2\le2\int_{\mathbb R}|z z_x|(s,y)\,ds=:A(y)$ and $|z(x,y)|^2\le2\int_{\mathbb R}|z z_y|(x,s)\,ds=:B(x)$. Thus $|z|^4\le A(y)B(x)$, and integration and Holder give $\|z\|_4^4\le4\|z\|_2^2\|z_x\|_2\|z_y\|_2\le2\|z\|_2^2\|\nabla z\|_2^2$. Apply this to components of a vector and to differences of compact smooth approximants defining $H^1_0(D)^2$, extended by zero. The inequality makes the approximants Cauchy in $L^4$, so their limit is the same $L^2$ function; consequently $\|z\|_4^2\le C\|z\|_2\|\nabla z\|_2$ on $H^1_0(D)^2$. Each energy velocity therefore belongs to $L^4_tL^4_x$.

With its $H^1$ inner product the complete space $H^1(D)^2$ is Hilbert. Its closed subspace $H^1_0(D)^2$ is Hilbert, as is $V_\sigma$, the kernel of bounded divergence therein. Poincare gives its equivalent gradient norm and [F2] gives reflexivity. Separability follows by mapping $H^1(D)^2$ isometrically, in its full norm, into the finite product of scalar $L^2$ spaces listing components and first derivatives. This product is separable by [F2]; every metric subspace of a separable metric space is separable: restrict a countable ambient base and, using Countable Choice, select a point from each nonempty restricted basic set. This proves separability of $V_\sigma$. The closure $H_\sigma$ is Hilbert as a closed $L^2$ subspace. Its inclusion of $V_\sigma$ is continuous by Poincare, injective and dense by definition. Thus the canonical pivot map $Jh(v)=(h,v)_2$ is bounded and injective and the triple has all hypotheses of [F3].

For a solenoidal energy velocity $u$, its convection functional on $V_\sigma$ is $N(u)(v)=-\int_D(u\otimes u):
abla v$, since the divergence and boundary terms vanish by approximation. Holder bounds its norm by $\|u\|_4^2$, which belongs to $L^2(0,T)$ by step 1.1. This is a strongly measurable dual-valued function: the map $L^4(D)^2	o V_\sigma^*$ is continuous and quadratic, and $u$ is strongly measurable in $L^4$ as a continuous image of its Bochner $V_\sigma$ representative. The viscous functional is a bounded linear image of $u\in L^2_tV_\sigma$, and the force functional is a bounded linear image of $f\in L^2_tL^2$. The fixed-test equation [F1] therefore says that the actual restricted derivative is the $L^2_tV_\sigma^*$ function $f-
u(
abla u,
abla\cdot)-N(u)$. Apply [F3] to obtain a unique strong $C([0,T];H_\sigma)$ representative and its energy chain rule. This representative agrees with the given weakly continuous one (fixed dense tests identify them), and so its initial value is $u_0$.

For two such velocities $u,\widetilde u$ with the same data let $z=u-\widetilde u$. Their difference has restricted derivative in $L^2_tV_\sigma^*$ by step 2.1, so [F3] permits pairing its equation with $z$ and differentiating its squared pivot norm. The trilinear cancellation leaves, with either velocity named $u$,
$$	frac12 rac{d}{dt}\|z\|_2^2+
u\|
abla z\|_2^2\le\left|\int_D(z\cdot
abla)u\cdot zight|\le C\|
abla u\|_2\|z\|_2\|
abla z\|_2\le	frac
u2\|
abla z\|_2^2+C
u^{-1}\|
abla u\|_2^2\|z\|_2^2.$$
The first estimate uses the planar bound in step 1.1; the final one is $ab\le
u a^2/2+C
u^{-1}b^2$. The initial difference is zero by step 2.1. Put $Y(t)=\|z(t)\|_2^2$ and $B(t)=C
u^{-1}\|
abla u(t)\|_2^2$, increasing the constant to absorb the factor $2$. The chain rule makes $Y$ absolutely continuous and gives $Y(t)\le Y(s)+\int_s^t B(r)Y(r)\,dr$, with $B\ge0$ in $L^1$. Choose $K>0$ with $\int_{\{B>K\}}B<1/4$ by [F4], and choose $\delta>0$ with $K\delta<1/4$. Partition $[0,T]$ into finitely many intervals of length at most $\delta$; each has $\int_I B<1/2$. On the first interval $Y(0)=0$ and continuity gives $\sup_IY\le(\sup_IY)\int_I B\le	frac12\sup_IY$, hence $Y=0$. Inductively the same argument applies on every next interval since its initial value is zero. Thus $z=0$ throughout $[0,T]$. This proves uniqueness and, together with the earlier steps, all stated regularity and trace assertions.

Positive viscosity and the stated Hilbert energy spaces are required.

risk_review.notes: All four steps checked against the evolution-triple definition and actual chain-rule proof, including strong endpoints. Closed divergence kernel is separable Hilbert by the derivative embedding into finite L2 products; pivot is its L2 closure. Planar L4 gives a strongly measurable L2 V-sigma* nonlinear functional. Finite small-integral partition forces zero norm difference. All arguments hold on bounded connected Lipschitz domains; removed the unnecessary polyhedral qualifier. No full V* derivative inferred.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d=2$ or $3$, be a bounded connected Lipschitz polygonal/polyhedral domain with a conforming shape-regular affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$. On a simplex $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_d$, define the scalar interior bubble $b_K=(d+1)^{d+1}\prod_{i=0}^d\lambda_i$. Let
$$S^1_h=\{w\in C^0(\overline D):w|_K\in P_1(K)\},\quad S^1_{h,0}=S^1_h\cap H^1_0(D).$$
The **mini-element spaces** are
$$V_h=[S^1_{h,0}]^d\oplus\bigoplus_{K\in\mathcal T_h}b_K\mathbb R^d\subset H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q_h=S^1_h\cap L^2_0(D).$$
Each bubble is extended by zero off its cell. The zero-boundary conformity of the piecewise affine part is supplied by [[thm-zero-boundary-piecewise-polynomials-in-w10p]]. The local/global dimensions are proved in the next dimension lemma.

Assume Countable Choice as inherited from the energy-space conventions. Interpret each interval forcing average as a Bochner integral; its existence follows from the stated L2 forcing and the Bochner integrability criterion ([[def-countable-choice]], [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]). Let $D$ be as in [[def-na-evolutionary-incompressible-ns-weak-solution]], let $\mathcal T_h$ be a conforming shape-regular affine simplicial mesh of $D$, and let $V_h,Q_h,Z_h$ be the MINI spaces and weak divergence kernel of [[def-na-mini-element-p1-bubble-p1-spaces]] and [[def-na-discrete-weak-and-exact-divergence-free-spaces]]. For a partition $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$, write $\tau_n=t_n-t_{n-1}$ and $f_h^n=\tau_n^{-1}\int_{t_{n-1}}^{t_n}f(t)\,dt$. Given $u_h^0\in Z_h$, a **backward Euler mini-element solution** is a sequence $(u_h^n,p_h^n)\in V_h\times Q_h$ satisfying, for $n=1,\ldots,N$,
$$\left(\frac{u_h^n-u_h^{n-1}}{\tau_n},v_h\right)_{L^2}+a_\nu(u_h^n,v_h)+c(u_h^n;u_h^n,v_h)+b(v_h,p_h^n)=(f_h^n,v_h)_{L^2}\quad(v_h\in V_h),$$
$$b(u_h^n,q_h)=0\quad(q_h\in Q_h).$$
All pressure variables use the zero-mean gauge $Q_h\subset L^2_0(D)$. Restriction to $v_h\in Z_h$ eliminates pressure. The equations are well-defined by [[lem-na-mini-be-scheme-is-well-defined]]; this definition claims no solver termination or error rate.

For the conforming mini-element spaces $V_h,Q_h$, define the **weak discrete divergence kernel** by
$$Z_h:=\{v_h\in V_h:b(v_h,q_h)=0\text{ for every }q_h\in Q_h\},$$
and the **exact discrete divergence kernel** by
$$Z_h^0:=\{v_h\in V_h:\operatorname{div}v_h=0\text{ almost everywhere on }D\}.$$
Since $b(v_h,q_h)=-\int_Dq_h\operatorname{div}v_h$, one has $Z_h^0\subseteq Z_h$. Equality is not part of either definition; the companion example proves strictness for a concrete mesh.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz open set, where Lipschitz means that $\partial D$ has a finite rigidly moved graph-chart atlas. Here $H^1_0(D)$ is the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(D)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). Since $D$ has finite measure, Holder makes every $L^2$ class integrable, so the zero-mean condition is well-defined ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]). Define
$$V:=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q:=L^2_0(D):=\{q\in L^2(D;\mathbb R):\int_Dq=0\}.$$
Equip $V$ with $\|v\|_V:=\|
abla v\|_{L^2(D)}$ and $Q$ with $\|q\|_Q:=\|q\|_{L^2(D)}$. The local Poincare inequality [[lem-na-homogeneous-dirichlet-poincare]] makes the first a norm equivalent to the usual $H^1$ norm. For $v\in V$, define $\varepsilon(v):=(
abla v+
abla v^T)/2$ and $b(v,q):=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v$. For viscosity $
u>0$, set $a_
u(u,v):=2
u\int_D\varepsilon(u):\varepsilon(v)$, where $X:Y=\sum_{i,j}X_{ij}Y_{ij}$. The continuous domain class is all bounded connected Lipschitz $D$; the exact mini-element mesh class is the narrower polygonal/polyhedral conforming affine simplicial class.

Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded connected Lipschitz domain with $d\in\{2,3\}$, and let $V=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ as in [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]]. For $a,b,c\in V$, define the real **skew convective form**
$$c(a;b,c):= rac12\int_D ig((a\cdot
abla)b\cdot c-(a\cdot
abla)c\cdot b ig)\,dx.$$
The middle and last slots are displayed separately to emphasize $c(a;b,c)=-c(a;c,b)$. In particular $c(a;b,b)=0$. The integrals are well-defined on $V$ by [[lem-na-evolutionary-skew-convective-form-bound]]. If additionally $\operatorname{div}a=0$, then $c(a;b,c)=\int_D(a\cdot
abla)b\cdot c$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V_h,Q_h$ be the stable mini-element spaces on a bounded connected Lipschitz polyhedral domain with a conforming mesh, with viscosity $\nu>0$, and let $Z_h=\{v_h:b(v_h,q_h)=0\ \forall q_h\in Q_h\}$. Choose bases of $V_h,Q_h$, let $M$ be the velocity mass matrix, $A$ the Stokes stiffness matrix, and $B$ the constraint matrix with entries $B_{\ell j}=b(\phi_j,\chi_\ell)$. The mass-orthogonal projector onto $Z_h$ is
$$P_M=I-M^{-1}B^T(BM^{-1}B^T)^{-1}B.$$
On the mean-zero pressure coordinates, both the mass pressure Schur matrix $BM^{-1}B^T$ and stiffness pressure Schur matrix $BA^{-1}B^T$ are positive definite. Before imposing the pressure gauge on the full continuous P1 space, the constant pressure is exactly the one-dimensional nullspace of $B^T$.

On the mini-element spaces of [[def-na-mini-element-p1-bubble-p1-spaces]], there is a Fortin operator $\Pi_h:V\to V_h$ preserving $b(v,q_h)$ for every $q_h\in Q_h$, with $\|\Pi_hv\|_V\le C_F\|v\|_V$. The constant depends only on $d$ and the mesh shape-regularity bound, not on $h$. Consequently
$$\beta_h\ge (C_FC_{\rm div}(D))^{-1}.$$

Assume Countable Choice, the mini-element hypotheses of [[def-na-mini-navier-stokes-backward-euler-scheme]], $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2(D)^d)$, and an initial value $u_h^0\in Z_h$. On every finite positive time partition there is at least one mixed solution $(u_h^n,p_h^n)_{n=1}^N$ of the backward Euler scheme. Every such solution satisfies, for $0\le m\le N$, the work-form inequality
$$ rac12\|u_h^m\|_2^2+ rac12\sum_{n=1}^m\|u_h^n-u_h^{n-1}\|_2^2+
u\sum_{n=1}^m	au_n\|
abla u_h^n\|_2^2\le rac12\|u_h^0\|_2^2+\sum_{n=1}^m	au_n(f_h^n,u_h^n)_{L^2}.$$
Consequently it satisfies the mesh-independent estimate
$$ rac12\|u_h^m\|_2^2+ rac12\sum_{n=1}^m\|u_h^n-u_h^{n-1}\|_2^2+ rac{
u}{2}\sum_{n=1}^m	au_n\|
abla u_h^n\|_2^2\le rac12\|u_h^0\|_2^2+ rac{C_P(D)^2}{2
u}\|f\|_{L^2(0,T;L^2)}^2.$$
The constant is independent of mesh size and time-step sizes.

Assume Countable Choice. For $d\in\{2,3\}$ and $V=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ on a bounded Lipschitz domain, the form in [[def-na-evolutionary-skew-convective-form]] is a continuous real trilinear map $V^3	o\mathbb R$, is skew in its last two slots, and satisfies
$$|c(a;b,w)|\le C_D\|a\|_{L^2}^{1/2}\|
abla a\|_{L^2}^{1/2}\|
abla b\|_{L^2}\|
abla w\|_{L^2}.$$
Consequently, if $u\in L^\infty(0,T;L^2)\cap L^2(0,T;V)$, then $c(u;u,\cdot)\in L^{4/3}(0,T;V^*)$. If $\operatorname{div}u=0$ and $d=2$, the sharper estimate
$$|c(u;u,w)|\le C_D\|u\|_{L^2}\|
abla u\|_{L^2}\|
abla w\|_{L^2}$$
holds. If $\operatorname{div}a=0$, the skew form agrees with the advective form $\int_D(a\cdot
abla)b\cdot w$.

Assume Countable Choice. For bounded open $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $v\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, put $\varepsilon(v)=(
abla v+
abla v^T)/2$. Then
$$2\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2^2=\|
abla v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2,$$
so $\|
abla v\|_2\le\sqrt2\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2$.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $C\subseteq H$ be closed and convex with $x\in H$, and let $p\in C$. Then $p$ is the nearest point of $C$ to $x$ if and only if

$$\operatorname{Re}\langle x-p,\ y-p\rangle\le0 \qquad \text{for every } y\in C .$$

In particular, for the nearest point the inequality holds, and conversely any $p\in C$ satisfying the inequality is nearest.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $p,q>1$ satisfy $1/p+1/q=1$. For $u,v\ge0$,
$$uv\le\frac{u^p}{p}+\frac{v^q}{q}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(f_n)$ be nonnegative measurable functions. Then
$$\int \liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let
$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y
otin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and
$$\int f\,d\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}=\int_X I_f\,d\mu=\int_Y J_f\,d
u.$$
2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes 
u})$, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the measure-theoretic
interfaces cited below. Let $d\ge1$, $0<s<1$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^d$ and
its sigma-algebra are those of
[[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]].

For a Lebesgue measurable $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb K$ put
$$[g]_{s,p}:=\Bigl(\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}|g(x)-g(y)|^p\,|x-y|^{-d-sp}\,dx\,dy\Bigr)^{1/p}\in[0,+\infty].$$
The integrand is read as $0$ on the diagonal $x=y$; the integral is the
nonnegative extended integral of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] over the
completed product measure $dx\,dy$ of
[[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]]. The **Gagliardo--
Slobodeckij space** of order $s$ and exponent $p$ is
$$W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb K):=\{g\in L^p(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb K):[g]_{s,p}<\infty\},$$
where $L^p(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb K)$ is the quotient of the measurable functions
by almost-everywhere equality
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]); its elements are classes,
and the space is normed by
$$\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^d)}:=\|g\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)}+[g]_{s,p}.$$
Write $[g]_{s,p}$ also for the value on a class, and call $[\cdot]_{s,p}$ the
**Slobodeckij seminorm**.

Three conventions are part of the definition. First, the diagonal
$\{(x,y):x=y\}$ is a Lebesgue-null subset of $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d$
(its section at every $x$ is a single point, so Tonelli gives product measure
zero), and on the diagonal the integrand is declared zero; thus the convention
changes the integrand only on a null set and does not affect the integral.
Second, the integral is a nonnegative extended integral, so $[g]_{s,p}=+\infty$
is allowed and $W^{s,p}$ is a set of $L^p$ classes with finite seminorm; the
difference $g(x)-g(y)$ is taken between representatives, and changing
representatives on a null set changes the integrand only on a null subset of
the product. Third, the definition is stated on classes but representative
independence is not assumed here: it is the first clause of
[[lem-slobodeckij-seminorm-is-well-defined]], the item that establishes that
this definition is well posed on $L^p$ classes. That the expression
$\|\cdot\|_{W^{s,p}}$ is a genuine norm, and that $W^{s,p}$ is a vector space,
are likewise proved there, not asserted as part of the definition.

On this page the case used is the trace exponent
$$s=\theta:=1-\frac1p\in(0,1),$$
which is available exactly for $1<p<\infty$. For that exponent the weight
simplifies to $|x-y|^{-d-p\theta}=|x-y|^{-d-(p-1)}$. The endpoint $p=1$ is
treated separately on this page and is never described by a space
$W^{0,1}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $0<\theta<1$,
$1\le p<\infty$ with $p\theta<d$ and $p_\star:=\frac{dp}{d-p\theta}$. There is
$C=C(d,p,\theta)>0$ such that every measurable, compactly supported
$f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ satisfies
$$\|f\|_{L^{p_\star}(\mathbb R^d)}^{p}\ \le\ C\,[f]_{\theta,p}^{p}.$$
Consequently, for every bounded open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and every
$1\le q\le p_\star$ there is $C'=C'(d,p,\theta,U,q)$ with
$\|f\|_{L^q(U)}\le C'\bigl(\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^d)}+[f]_{\theta,p}\bigr)$ for
every compactly supported measurable $f$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $1<p<\infty$, $\theta=1-1/p$,
$H=\mathbb R^d\times(0,\infty)$, and let $T_+$ be the half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]]. Write
$|Du|^p:=\sum_{j=1}^{d+1}|D_ju|^p$ for the sum of the $p$-th powers of the
weak first derivatives, and $[\cdot]_{\theta,p}$ for the Slobodeckij seminorm
of [[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]. Then for every
$u\in W^{1,p}(H;\mathbb K)$ with $g=T_+u$,
$$[g]_{\theta,p}^p\le C(d,p)\int_H|Du|^p\,dx=C(d,p)\sum_{j=1}^{d+1}\|D_ju\|_{L^p(H)}^p\le C(d,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(H)}^p;$$
equivalently $T_+:W^{1,p}(H;\mathbb K)\to W^{\theta,p}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb K)$
is a bounded operator.

The homogeneous estimate is scale invariant: for $r>0$ and
$u_r(x',t):=u(rx',rt)$ one has $g_{u_r}(x')=g(rx')$ and
$$[g_{u_r}]_{\theta,p}^p=r^{-d+p\theta}[g]_{\theta,p}^p,\qquad \int_H|Du_r|^p\,dx=r^{-d+p\theta}\int_H|Du|^p\,dx,$$
because $p\theta=p-1$; so both sides of the homogeneous estimate scale with
the same exponent $r^{-d+p\theta}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, bounded, convex and nonempty, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u-u_\Omega\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(n)\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Here $u_\Omega=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u\,dx$ is the mean of $u$ over $\Omega$,
which is well defined because $\Omega$ is nonempty open and bounded. The proof
below gives the explicit choice
$$C(n)=\frac{2\,(2^n-1)}{n},$$
which depends only on the dimension; no dependence on $p$, on the shape of
$\Omega$, on $|\Omega|$ or on the regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $1<p<\infty$ and let $f:(0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable, with
$Hf(t):=t^{-1}\int_0^t f(s)\,ds$. Then
$$\Bigl(\int_0^\infty\bigl(Hf(t)\bigr)^p\,dt\Bigr)^{1/p}\le\frac{p}{p-1}\Bigl(\int_0^\infty f(s)^p\,ds\Bigr)^{1/p},$$
equivalently
$$\int_0^\infty t^{-p}\Bigl(\int_0^t f(s)\,ds\Bigr)^pdt\le\Bigl(\frac{p}{p-1}\Bigr)^p\int_0^\infty f(s)^p\,ds,$$
where both sides are extended nonnegative integrals and $+\infty$ is allowed on
either side. The constant $p/(p-1)$ is sharp: for every $c<p/(p-1)$ there is a
measurable $f$ with $\|Hf\|_{L^p}>c\|f\|_{L^p}$. If $f$ is supported in
$(0,T)$ for some $0<T<\infty$, then the same inequality holds on $(0,T)$,
$$\int_0^T t^{-p}\Bigl(\int_0^t f(s)\,ds\Bigr)^pdt\le\Bigl(\frac{p}{p-1}\Bigr)^p\int_0^T f(s)^p\,ds,$$
with the same constant.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For all
$f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$,

$$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)} ,$$where both sums are taken in the finite-subset-supremum/finite-subset-net sense of [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. The bilinear series is absolutely convergent,$$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\bigl|\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}\bigr|\le \Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\widehat f(k)|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} \Bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|\widehat g(k)|^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

and the value is also the limit of the canonical symmetric partial sums
$\sum_{|k|\le N}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For every
$f\in L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$ and every real $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$N\in\mathbb N$ with

$$\Bigl\|f-\sum_{|k|\le N}\widehat f(k)e_k\Bigr\|_2<\varepsilon .$$

Thus the symmetric partial sums of the Fourier series converge to $f$ in the
$L^2$ norm, and the finite-subset net of Fourier partial sums converges to $f$
as well. This is norm convergence only: no pointwise or uniform assertion is
made, and no ordering of $\mathbb Z$ other than the symmetric one is required.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^n$ be open, let
$f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $(a,b)\in U$ satisfy $f(a,b)=0$.
Assume the complex Jacobian with respect to the second block is invertible:

$$\det\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial w_k}(a,b)\right)_{1\le j,k\le n}\ne0.$$

Then there are neighbourhoods $A$ of $a$ and $B$ of $b$, and a unique
holomorphic map $\varphi:A\to B$, such that

$$f(z,\varphi(z))=0\qquad(z\in A),$$

and, after shrinking $A\times B$ if needed,

$$f(z,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=\varphi(z).$$

Let $C(a,r)$ be a positively oriented circle, and let $f$ be meromorphic on a
neighbourhood of the closed disc $\overline{D(a,r)}$ with no pole on the circle.
Then

$\int_{C(a,r)}f(z)\,dz=2\pi i\sum_{|b-a|<r}\operatorname{Res}(f,b),$

the sum being over the poles of $f$ inside the circle.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

derivations.claim: We first establish the internal claims needed by the construction, and then make one simultaneous parameter choice and apply them. A conditional estimate in an internal claim is used only after its stated geometric or source premise is proved in a later phase. For bounded Hilbert sequences below, weak subsequences can be obtained without an unstated compactness supplier: work in the closure of the countable union of the finite spaces involved and the fixed data, choose a countable dense set, extract successively convergent scalar pairings by interval bisection, and take the diagonal subsequence. Its bounded limiting functional extends by density and is represented by Riesz; norm lower semicontinuity follows by testing against that representative. For an exterior exhaustion the countable nodal bases and bounded-radius cutoffs give the same separable subspace.

Two elementary inequalities used below have direct local proofs. For zero-boundary smooth scalar functions on $\mathbb R^2$, integrate $\partial_x|v|^2$ and $\partial_y|v|^2$ along the coordinate lines, multiply the two bounds, integrate and apply Cauchy–Schwarz to obtain $\|v\|_4^2\le2\|v\|_2\|\nabla v\|_2$; density and componentwise application give the same estimate for every $H^1_0$ vector, irrespective of its divergence. These prove the fractional Poincare and Ladyzhenskaya uses in the internal claims.

Fix a scale $r>0$, the rectangle $C=[-4r,4r]\times[0,4r]$, and the lower triangle with vertices $(-4r,0),(0,-4r),(4r,0)$. Their union is the fixed convex pentagon $D$. **Part 2: Finite recursive geometry and all boundary-star budgets.** **1. Scales and the true outer-radius restriction**. Let the parent fan radius be H, aperture a_p, and tooth count N. A straight main tooth side has root distance `D comparable to a_p H/N.` Choose selected attachment centers on its middle thirds at spacing ell comparable to b0 D. The child half-container is, in local tangent/normal coordinates, `C_r=[-4r,4r]x[0,4r],   r comparable to sigma ell.` Choose the already free dyadic strip height with 0<epsilon_strip<=c a_c. Its base contains exactly c_-=(-4r,0), o=(0,0), c_+=(4r,0); its other four boundary nodes are (±4r,epsilon_strip r),(±4r,4r). These seven nodes and all seven boundary edges remain unchanged under every descendant replacement. The clearance from an attachment to nonincident tooth sides is at least cD, but SAME-SIDE neighboring children are only distance comparable to ell apart. Thus a single-child ring must use outer scale `R comparable to c0 ell,      r/R comparable to sigma,     (1)` with c0 a sufficiently small fixed constant. **2. The actual uniform ring and its transition**. Use local square coordinates on the exterior half-plane. Let S_s=[-s,s]x[0,s]. Keep the actual child C_r inside S_(8r). Increase the integer k if needed; no lower bound on d is imposed. This in particular implies the required d<=Cr²/R. R/r is dyadic, so every boundary of S_(8r) and S_(4R) is a union of lattice edges. Thus, with the cutoff parameter r_tr=16r, the common annuli 2r_tr through 8r_tr and their one-cell enlargements are entirely uniform, provided R is chosen larger than a fixed multiple of r. **3. Keeping every long child edge unrefined**.
